triage.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
triage.reason: Term or near-term infant, often after cesarean delivery, with early tachypnea that resolves; a classic neonatal respiratory distress look-alike reachable by history, exam and chest x-ray.

demographics: More common after cesarean delivery, especially elective cesarean without labor

risk_factors.text: Cesarean delivery, especially scheduled before labor begins

chief_complaints.text: My baby is grunting and working hard to breathe
My baby's nose is flaring with each breath

hpi.onset: Within the first few hours after birth, usually by 1–2 hours of life
hpi.duration: Typically resolves within 24–72 hours; tachypnea is present from birth and gradually improves
hpi.progression: Respiratory rate is highest in the first hours, then slowly falls; oxygen need, if any, decreases over 1–3 days
hpi.quality: Rapid, shallow breathing with grunting, nasal flaring and retractions
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually no need for mechanical ventilation
hpi.timing: Continuous from birth, improving over 1–3 days

associated_symptoms.text: Mild cyanosis or low oxygen saturation

atypical.how_it_differs: Late-preterm infants may have milder tachypnea but more feeding difficulty and a longer course; term infants after vaginal delivery may have a very brief episode that resolves within hours.
Not applicable; this condition occurs only in newborns.

general.mild: Alert, well-perfused newborn with mild tachypnea; no distress at rest
general.moderate: Tachypneic with visible work of breathing (grunting, flaring, retractions); consolable
general.severe: Marked tachypnea with prominent grunting and retractions; may need supplemental oxygen
general.critical: Respiratory failure with apnea or need for mechanical ventilation; ill-appearing

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute while the infant is calm
Auscultate over the trachea or observe the infant at rest
Observe the chest wall during inspiration

findings.finding: Fine inspiratory crackles at the bases
Lungs clear to auscultation without crackles or wheezing

findings.maneuver: Assess muscle tone by passive movement of the limbs

findings.finding: Pink, well-perfused with capillary refill less than 3 seconds

labs.caveat: Neonatal reference ranges are higher than adult ranges and vary with age in hours; a mild leukocytosis is common in TTN and does not by itself indicate infection. A normal or low white count with an elevated immature-to-total neutrophil ratio is more concerning for sepsis.
Band forms are normally higher in the first days of life; marked bandemia or a high immature-to-total neutrophil ratio suggests sepsis rather than TTN.
May rise mildly with the stress of labor and delivery; a normal CRP at 24–48 hours supports TTN over bacterial infection, but a single early value does not exclude sepsis.
Hypoglycemia is common in newborns with respiratory distress and poor feeding and must be corrected; it is not specific to TTN.

Mild respiratory acidosis with CO2 retention can occur with marked tachypnea and work of breathing; severe or persistent acidosis should prompt reconsideration of sepsis, pneumonia or a cardiac lesion.
Mild hypoxemia is common; profound or refractory hypoxemia argues against TTN.

imaging.preferred_when: All newborns with tachypnea or respiratory distress; the key study for distinguishing TTN from other causes

findings.text: Prominent central pulmonary vascular markings radiating from the hila
Perihilar streaking or perihilar interstitial edema
Mild symmetric hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms
Fluid in the minor fissure or interlobar fissures
Normal or near-normal lung volumes with clear peripheral lung fields

imaging.preferred_when: When a cardiac cause is suspected (murmur, differential cyanosis, weak or absent femoral pulses, shock, or hypoxemia out of proportion to the lung findings)

findings.text: Persistent fetal circulation pattern with right-to-left shunting if pulmonary pressures remain elevated
Structural congenital heart disease (e.g., coarctation, transposition, total anomalous pulmonary venous return) — an alternative diagnosis, not TTN

imaging.preferred_when: Any newborn with respiratory distress in whom sepsis or pneumonia cannot be excluded; obtained before starting antibiotics

findings.text: Growth of a pathogen (e.g., group B Streptococcus, E. coli) — indicates sepsis or pneumonia rather than TTN

initial.why: First-line study; shows the hyperinflation, perihilar streaking and fluid in the fissures typical of TTN and helps exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, meconium aspiration and congenital heart disease
Baseline white count and differential; a normal count with a low immature-to-total neutrophil ratio supports TTN over sepsis
Detects hypoglycemia, which is common in distressed newborns and requires treatment
Obtained before antibiotics when sepsis or pneumonia cannot be excluded
initial.only_if: sepsis or pneumonia is suspected (fever, hypothermia, lethargy, risk factors such as maternal fever, chorioamnionitis or prolonged rupture of membranes)

initial.why: Assesses oxygenation and ventilation in infants with significant distress or oxygen requirement
initial.only_if: moderate to severe distress or a rising oxygen requirement

supporting.why: A normal value at 24–48 hours supports a benign course; a rising value suggests infection
Excludes structural congenital heart disease and assesses pulmonary pressures
supporting.only_if: a cardiac cause is suspected (murmur, differential cyanosis, weak femoral pulses, shock, or hypoxemia out of proportion to lung findings)

not_indicated.why: Routine electrolytes are not needed for uncomplicated TTN; order only if the infant is receiving IV fluids or has poor intake
Not part of the routine evaluation of TTN; reserve for suspected shock or sepsis
Not routinely used in newborns; evidence for its role in neonatal sepsis is limited
CT of the chest is not used in newborns with suspected TTN; it adds radiation without changing management
Not routine in an otherwise well newborn with classic TTN findings and no cardiac signs
Not needed if the infant is well-appearing with a classic TTN picture and no sepsis risk factors

decision_points: Distinguish TTN from respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia/sepsis, meconium aspiration and congenital heart disease using the chest x-ray, risk factors and clinical course
Start empiric antibiotics when sepsis or pneumonia cannot be excluded, then stop them if cultures are negative and the infant improves within 48–72 hours
Reassess if tachypnea persists beyond 72 hours or worsens — this should prompt evaluation for another cause
Check glucose in any distressed newborn and treat hypoglycemia promptly

differential.name: Respiratory distress syndrome
differential.why_considered: Early tachypnea with grunting, retractions and oxygen requirement in a newborn
differential.trigger: Preterm or late-preterm infant with worsening distress and increasing oxygen need over the first hours

history: Distress that worsens rather than improves over the first 24 hours
exam: May progress to apnea or need for continuous positive airway pressure or mechanical ventilation
labs: Respiratory acidosis with CO2 retention on blood gas
Hypoxemia that responds poorly to supplemental oxygen
imaging: Low lung volumes with a bell-shaped chest

differential.name: Neonatal pneumonia or sepsis
differential.why_considered: Tachypnea and respiratory distress in a newborn can be the first sign of infection
differential.trigger: Maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes, foul-smelling fluid, or an ill-appearing infant with fever, hypothermia or lethargy

history: Fever, hypothermia, lethargy or poor feeding
labs: Elevated or low white blood cell count with a high immature-to-total neutrophil ratio
imaging: Lobar or diffuse infiltrates rather than perihilar streaking

differential.name: Meconium aspiration syndrome
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress in a term or post-term newborn with tachypnea and oxygen requirement
differential.trigger: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid at delivery with a distressed infant

exam: Meconium staining of the skin, nails and umbilical cord
Marked respiratory distress with a barrel-shaped chest
imaging: Areas of atelectasis and air leak (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum)

differential.name: Congenital heart disease
differential.why_considered: Tachypnea and cyanosis in a newborn can be caused by a structural cardiac lesion
differential.trigger: Murmur, differential cyanosis, weak or absent femoral pulses, shock, or hypoxemia out of proportion to the lung findings

history: Cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen
Family history of congenital heart disease
Feeding difficulty and poor weight gain
imaging: Abnormal cardiac silhouette or pulmonary vascularity on chest x-ray

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden tachypnea and respiratory distress in a newborn

history: History of resuscitation, positive-pressure ventilation or meconium aspiration
exam: Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
Shifted heart sounds or tracheal deviation
imaging: Air in the pleural space with lung collapse
Mediastinal shift away from the affected side

differential.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
differential.why_considered: Respiratory distress in a newborn with tachypnea and cyanosis

exam: Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
Bowel sounds heard in the chest
imaging: Mediastinal shift to the opposite side

severity.mild: Respiratory rate 60–80/min with minimal or no grunting or retractions; room air oxygen saturation above 95%; feeding well; resolves within 24–48 hours
severity.moderate: Respiratory rate 70–90/min with grunting, nasal flaring and retractions; mild oxygen requirement (saturation 90–95% on low-flow oxygen); resolves within 48–72 hours
severity.severe: Respiratory rate 80–100/min with marked work of breathing; oxygen requirement with saturation 85–92% on supplemental oxygen; may need continuous positive airway pressure; resolves over 3–5 days
severity.critical: Respiratory failure with apnea or need for mechanical ventilation; rare in TTN and should prompt reconsideration of another diagnosis such as sepsis, pneumonia or congenital heart disease

red_flags.finding: Apnea or recurrent pauses in breathing
red_flags.meaning: Suggests sepsis, respiratory distress syndrome or another serious cause rather than uncomplicated TTN
Suggests infection (sepsis or pneumonia) and warrants a full sepsis evaluation and antibiotics
Suggests sepsis, hypoglycemia or a metabolic cause; needs urgent evaluation
TTN should be resolving; consider pneumonia, congenital heart disease or another diagnosis
Suggests congenital heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension rather than TTN

red_flags.finding: Weak or absent femoral pulses or a cardiac murmur

red_flags.meaning: Suggests a gastrointestinal or surgical cause rather than TTN

complications.name: Hypoglycemia
clues: Low blood glucose on point-of-care testing

complications.name: Feeding difficulty and poor weight gain
Respiratory acidosis
clues: Marked tachypnea with CO2 retention on blood gas

special_populations.differences: Late-preterm infants may have milder tachypnea but more feeding difficulty and a longer course; term infants after vaginal delivery may have a very brief episode that resolves within hours.
Not applicable; this condition occurs only in newborns.

key_questions.question: How was your baby delivered — vaginally or by cesarean, and was it scheduled before labor started?
key_questions.looking_for: Cesarean delivery, especially elective cesarean before labor, is the strongest risk factor for delayed fetal lung fluid clearance

key_questions.question: How many weeks pregnant were you when you delivered?
key_questions.looking_for: Term or late preterm (34–37 weeks); prematurity raises concern for respiratory distress syndrome

key_questions.question: When did the fast breathing start?
key_questions.looking_for: Within the first few hours of life, usually by 1–2 hours; onset from birth rather than later

key_questions.question: Has the breathing gotten better, worse, or stayed the same since it started?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual improvement over hours to days; worsening distress suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Is the baby grunting, flaring the nostrils, or pulling in at the ribs?
key_questions.looking_for: Grunting, nasal flaring and retractions — signs of work of breathing that are usually mild in TTN

key_questions.question: Is the baby feeding well and keeping feeds down?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild feeding difficulty from tachypnea; bilious vomiting or abdominal distension suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any pauses in breathing or turned blue?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea or cyanosis argues against uncomplicated TTN and suggests sepsis, respiratory distress syndrome or cardiac disease

key_questions.question: Did you have a fever, chills, or an infection around the time of delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal fever or chorioamnionitis raises concern for neonatal sepsis or pneumonia

key_questions.question: How long was your water broken before delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged rupture of membranes (over 18 hours) increases the risk of infection

key_questions.question: Was the amniotic fluid clear, or was there meconium?
key_questions.looking_for: Meconium-stained fluid suggests meconium aspiration syndrome rather than TTN

key_questions.question: Were you told the baby had any problems during labor or needed help breathing right after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Resuscitation or positive-pressure ventilation, which raises concern for air leak or other causes

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or asthma, or was the baby large for gestational age?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal diabetes or asthma and macrosomia are weak risk factors for TTN

key_questions.question: Is the baby a boy or a girl?
key_questions.looking_for: Male sex is a weak risk factor for TTN

reasoning_points: Term or late-preterm newborn with tachypnea beginning within the first few hours of life
Often delivered by cesarean, especially elective cesarean before labor, consistent with delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid
Mild to moderate work of breathing (grunting, nasal flaring, retractions) with no fever, lethargy or apnea
Chest x-ray shows prominent perihilar streaking, central vascular markings, mild hyperinflation and sometimes small pleural effusions or fluid in the fissures
No focal consolidation, no air leak and no abnormal cardiac silhouette
Sepsis and pneumonia considered and excluded or treated empirically until cultures are negative
Respiratory distress improves and tachypnea resolves within 24–72 hours without escalation of support
Alternative diagnoses such as respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration, congenital heart disease and pneumothorax are considered and argued against

easy: Term infant born by elective cesarean with tachypnea starting in the first hours of life
Mild grunting and nasal flaring with oxygen saturation above 95% on room air
Chest x-ray with classic perihilar streaking and fluid in the fissures
medium: Late-preterm infant with milder tachypnea but prominent feeding difficulty and a longer course
Mild oxygen requirement with saturation 90–95% on low-flow oxygen
Small pleural effusions or mild hyperinflation on chest x-ray
Sepsis risk factors present, requiring empiric antibiotics until cultures are negative
hard: Infant with tachypnea that persists beyond 72 hours, prompting reconsideration of pneumonia, congenital heart disease or another cause
Hypoxemia out of proportion to the lung findings, raising concern for structural heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension
Sudden worsening of respiratory status suggesting pneumothorax or air leak
Ill-appearing infant with fever or hypothermia and lethargy, where sepsis must be excluded before TTN can be diagnosed
